conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode; helpers: highest(x,n)/lowest(x,n), atr(n), swingHigh(k)/swingLow(k) = k-th most recent confirmed pivot, trendLine(...) = projected line value at bar 0

candidates.name: SwingPivot
candidates.quote: Trend lines can be drawn using swing points or best fit techniques such as linear regression calculations or simply quickly drawing a best approximation.
candidates.description: Primitive: a swing low is a bar whose low is below the lows of the pivotStrength bars on each side; a swing high is the mirror. Confirmed pivotStrength bars after the pivot bar.
candidates.pseudocode: isSwingLow(i) = low[i] < lowest(low, pivotStrength) over bars i+1..i+pivotStrength && low[i] < lowest(low, pivotStrength) over bars i-pivotStrength..i-1; swingLow(1) = most recent i >= pivotStrength with isSwingLow(i)

complexity.reason: swing-pivot detection with a confirmation lag; needs a scan back over a variable-length window

notes: Brooks never states a pivot strength; 2 bars each side is a reading of a 'minor swing point'. Every trend-line candidate below depends on this.

candidates.name: BullTrendLine
candidates.quote: A bull trend line is a line drawn across the lows of a bull trend, and a bear trend line is drawn across the highs of a bear trend.
candidates.description: The bull trend line is the straight line through the two most recent confirmed swing lows (second higher than first), projected to the current bar; the bear trend line is the mirror across swing highs.
candidates.pseudocode: p1 = swingLow(2); p2 = swingLow(1); require p2.price > p1.price; slope = (p2.price - p1.price) / (p2.bar - p1.bar); trendLine[0] = p2.price + slope * (0 - p2.bar)

complexity.reason: trend-line projection from two detected pivots; the line only exists a few bars after the second pivot is confirmed

candidates.name: BuyAtBullTrendLineTouch
candidates.quote: Every time the market pulls back to the area around the trend line, even if it undershoots or overshoots the trend line, look for a reversal off of the trend line and then enter in the direction of the trend.
candidates.description: In a bull trend, a bar dips to (or within tolerance of) the projected bull trend line and closes back above it; buy at the next open.
candidates.pseudocode: low[0] <= trendLine[0] + touchTolAtr * atr(atrLength) && close[0] > trendLine[0]
candidates.book_order_type: limit order at or slightly below the trend line, or stop above the bull reversal bar's high

complexity.reason: needs the projected trend-line value at the current bar

notes: Same idea as the Chapter 15 mined file's BuyAtBullTrendLineTouch (T15-13); kept self-contained here since it is this chapter's headline setup.

candidates.name: TrendLineTestExtremeAfterBreak
candidates.quote: Even after a trend line breaks, if it has been in effect for dozens of bars, the chances are high that the trend extreme will get tested after a pullback.
candidates.description: After a mature trend line (in effect at least matureBars bars) breaks, bias entries toward expecting one more test of the trend's extreme (highest high of the trend) before treating the trend as reversed, rather than immediately trading the break as a reversal.

complexity.reason: 'trend line age' requires persisting the line's start bar across redraws -- deciding when a trend line is 'the same line' versus a new one is a design decision, not just its projected value

candidates.name: TrendLineBreakStrengthPredictsReversal
candidates.quote: The strength of the trend line break provides an indication of the strength of the countertrend traders. The bigger and faster the countertrend move, the more likely that a reversal will occur, but there will usually first be a test of the trend's extreme.
candidates.description: The size/speed of the bar(s) breaking the trend line, relative to ATR, gates how much weight to give a subsequent reversal read; a small/slow break favors trend continuation, a large fast break favors an eventual (but not immediate) reversal.
candidates.pseudocode: breakBarRange = high[breakBar] - low[breakBar]; breakStrength = breakBarRange / atr(atrLength)

complexity.reason: Brooks gives no threshold, and the correct action is conditional on a subsequent extreme test (T13-04), not an immediate trade; the threshold and resulting action are a design decision

candidates.name: GapOrLargeTrendBarIsOneBarTrend
candidates.quote: It is helpful to consider a gap opening and any large trend bar to be effectively breakouts and each should be treated as if it is a one-bar trend, since breakouts commonly fail and you need to be prepared to fade them if there is a setup.
candidates.description: Primitive: a session gap-open, or any single bar whose range exceeds a multiple of ATR, is treated as its own miniature one-bar trend, whose 'trend line' is simply that bar's own extreme (its low for a bull one-bar trend).
candidates.pseudocode: isOneBarTrend(i) = (high[i] - low[i]) >= largeBarAtrMultiple * atr(atrLength) || isSessionGap(i); oneBarTrendLine = low[i]

complexity.reason: a single-bar ATR (or session-gap) test; the 'trend line' is just that bar's own extreme, no pivot search needed

candidates.name: FadeSidewaysBreakOfOneBarTrend
candidates.quote: Since the sideways bars broke the steep trend line, you can look to fade the trend if there is a good signal bar for the reversal.
candidates.description: After a one-bar trend (T13-06), sideways bars that close through its extreme (a break of the one-bar trend line) followed by a reversal-quality signal bar set up a countertrend fade.
candidates.pseudocode: isOneBarTrend(k) && close[0] < low[k] && close[0] > open[0] && (close[0] - open[0]) >= bodyFraction * (high[0] - low[0]) /* reversal bar, mirrored fade */
candidates.book_order_type: stop one tick beyond the reversal bar (mechanized: next bar open)

complexity.reason: needs the one-bar-trend flag and its extreme persisted from bar k, plus a reversal-bar test

candidates.name: RepeatedTrendLineTestsPrecedeBreakOrAccelerate
candidates.quote: If the market repeatedly tests a trend line many times in a relatively small number of bars and the market cannot drift far from that trend line, then either of two things will likely happen. Most of the time, the market will break through the trend line ... However, sometimes ... the trend accelerates rather than reverses.
candidates.description: Context: count how many times price has touched (within tolerance) the projected trend line within the last windowBars; a high touch count flags an imminent break-or-accelerate decision point rather than a routine pullback.
candidates.pseudocode: touchCount = countTrue(abs(low[i] - trendLine[i]) <= touchTolAtr * atr(atrLength) for i in 0..windowBars-1); touchCount >= minTouches

complexity.reason: needs the projected trend line evaluated at every bar in a window plus a touch counter

candidates.name: EachSuccessiveTrendLineFlatter
candidates.quote: Typically, each successive line has a flatter slope, indicating that the trend is losing momentum. At some point, trend lines in the opposite direction will become more important as control of the market switches.
candidates.description: Track the slope of successive redrawn trend lines (each anchored at the newest pivot after a break); a monotonically flattening slope sequence signals a maturing/weakening trend and rising odds that an opposite-direction trend line will soon dominate.
candidates.pseudocode: slope(currentTL) < slope(priorTL) * flattenFraction, tracked across successive redraws

complexity.reason: requires persisting a history of redrawn trend lines and their slopes, and a design decision on exactly when a 'redraw' occurs -- this is a trend-maturity read, not a single test

candidates.name: SecondAttemptToReverseTrendLineBreakout
candidates.quote: Bar 6 was a second attempt to reverse the break above that line and therefore a good short setup.
candidates.description: A second failed attempt to hold beyond a trend/channel line, after an initial failed attempt, is a higher-probability countertrend entry than the first attempt -- the second-entry principle applied to a line test.
candidates.book_order_type: stop one tick beyond the second reversal bar (mechanized: next bar open)

complexity.reason: combines the trend-line projection with the second-entry counting pattern over a derived per-bar test

notes: Generic form: Chapter 10's SecondReversalSignal, applied here to touches of a projected line instead of a fixed reversal-bar classification alone.

candidates.name: DuelingLinesConfluence
candidates.quote: This is where a trend channel line in a pullback or a leg of a channel intersects the channel's trend line.
candidates.description: Confluence filter: a signal bar is stronger when a smaller, locally drawn trend/channel line (e.g., of the current pullback) intersects the larger channel's trend line at roughly the same price -- two independently drawn lines 'dueling' at the same level.

complexity.reason: requires two independently anchored trend-line objects; choosing the smaller line's anchors (which pullback, which pivots) is a discretionary design decision

candidates.name: BestFitLineOnBodiesIgnoringTails
candidates.quote: Sometimes the best fit trend line is drawn just using the candle bodies and ignoring the tails; this is common in wedge patterns, which often do not have a wedge shape.
candidates.description: Variant trend-line construction: fit the line through the bodies of the anchor bars (min(open,close) for a bull line, max(open,close) for a bear line) instead of their tails.

complexity.reason: choosing bodies vs. tails per anchor bar is itself a discretionary read; Brooks gives no rule for when to prefer one over the other

candidates.name: LargeOverlapSignalsTradingRange
candidates.quote: the second, third, and fourth bars were large and almost entirely overlapping, and this is a sign of uncertainty, one of the hallmarks of a trading range.
candidates.description: When consecutive large bars overlap heavily (their ranges mostly coincide), treat the market as two-sided/trading-range rather than trending, and discount trend-line breakout signals formed by such bars.
candidates.pseudocode: (min(high[0], high[1]) - max(low[0], low[1])) >= overlapFraction * min(high[0] - low[0], high[1] - low[1]) && (high[0] - low[0]) >= largeBarAtrMultiple * atr(atrLength)

complexity.reason: a two-bar overlap ratio plus an ATR size test

notes: Opposite reading of the LittleOverlap primitive used elsewhere for spike bars (large overlap here signals a range, not a spike).

candidates.name: SessionMoveNearAverageDailyRangeExhaustion
candidates.quote: The average daily range was about 20 points, so once the market got down to about 20 points below the open, this gave traders another reason to look for a bounce.
candidates.description: Intraday filter: once the session's move from the open reaches close to the recent average daily range (from daily bars), treat further movement as exhausted and favor countertrend/reversal setups over continuation.

complexity.reason: needs a daily-bar average range computed alongside the intraday series (a multi-timeframe read) plus a session-open reference

rejected.quote: the market's direction is usually only about 50 percent certain because the bulls and bears are in balance most of the time... when there is a strong trend, traders can often be 60 percent or more certain of the direction.
rejected.reason: general probability commentary, no bar-level test.

rejected.quote: they are ignoring two other essential considerations for every trade: the risk and the probability of success. All three must be evaluated before placing a trade.
rejected.reason: general trading philosophy, no bar-level test.

rejected.quote: In actual practice, when you see a possible trend line and you are not certain how far it is from the current bar, draw it to see if the market has hit it and then quickly erase the line.
rejected.reason: manual charting workflow advice, not a bar-level condition.

chapter_summary: Chapter 13 mechanizes the bull/bear trend line as a line through two confirmed swing pivots, and builds the core with-trend pullback entry (buy the touch, T13-03) plus a family of context filters around how trend lines behave: mature lines get one more test of the extreme before reversing, break strength and repeated-touch counts hint at what comes next, successive redrawn lines flatten as a trend matures, and a second failed reversal attempt at a line is a stronger signal than the first. It also captured Brooks's 'gap or large bar is a one-bar trend' idea and a large-overlap trading-range sign. Several ideas (line age tracking, redraw state, dueling-lines confluence, bodies-vs-tails anchoring) are graded research because they need a persisted trend-line object and design decisions MINING.md flags as out of scope for this pass.
